content: Measles is an infectious disease caused by the Morbillivirus, a member of the Paramyxoviridae family. The virus is transmitted through respiratory secretions, such as aerosolized droplets, when an infected person coughs or sneezes. The incubation period for measles ranges from 4 to 12 days, during which the infected individual remains asymptomatic. The disease becomes symptomatic with the onset of a characteristic rash. Individuals with measles are contagious from five days before the rash appears until four days after its onset. The measles virus was first isolated in cell culture in 1954 by John F. Enders and Thomas C. Peebles. This breakthrough enabled the development of the first successful measles vaccine, which was licensed in 1963. To date, 21 distinct strains of the measles virus have been identified. Measles is caused by a nonsegmented, negative-stranded RNA virus. The primary site of infection is the respiratory epithelium of the nasopharynx. The virus spreads through respiratory secretions, particularly aerosolized droplets containing viral particles. Clinically, measles is characterized by a triad of symptoms: cough, coryza (runny nose), and conjunctivitis (red eyes). In most cases, the diagnosis can be made based on clinical presentation. However, differential diagnoses should be considered, including other viral exanthems such as erythema infectiosum, rubella, and maculopapular rashes. Atypical measles, which may occur in individuals vaccinated with killed vaccines, can present with fever, conjunctivitis, pneumonitis, and rash. Other conditions to consider in the differential diagnosis include Kawasaki disease, dengue fever, systemic lupus erythematosus, and serum sickness. Measles remains a leading cause of vaccine-preventable childhood mortality worldwide, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Global efforts, including the Measles Initiative, have significantly reduced measles-related deaths. Between 1999 and 2005, global measles deaths decreased by 60%, with the most notable progress in Africa, where annual deaths fell by 75% over five years. In developed countries, measles incidence is low, but lack of vaccination remains a significant risk factor. Most cases in countries like the United States are linked to unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated travelers. Primary vaccine failure occurs in approximately 5% of individuals vaccinated with a single dose at 12 months of age or older, increasing their susceptibility to measles. Measles is highly contagious, spreading through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes. The virus can survive on surfaces for up to two hours. Complications are common and range from mild conditions like diarrhea to severe outcomes such as pneumonia and encephalitis, including subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). Adults are more likely to experience severe complications. Approximately 6-20% of measles cases result in ear infections, diarrhea, or pneumonia. Encephalitis occurs in about 1 in 1,000 cases, and the mortality rate is also approximately 1 in 1,000. The diagnosis of measles is confirmed in individuals with febrile rash illness and either laboratory confirmation or an epidemiologic link to a confirmed case. Symptoms typically begin 7-14 days after infection. Clinical diagnosis requires a history of fever lasting at least three days, along with at least one of the three Cs: cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. Koplik's spots, small white lesions on the buccal mucosa, are a hallmark finding. Fever may reach up to 104°F (40°C). Physical examination findings include fever, rash, and conjunctivitis. Laboratory confirmation is essential for sporadic cases and outbreaks. Detection of measles-specific IgM antibodies and measles RNA via real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) are the most common diagnostic methods. Serum and throat or nasopharyngeal swabs should be collected at the first patient encounter. Urine samples may also contain the virus and can increase diagnostic yield when combined with respiratory samples. Chest X-rays may reveal patchy consolidation and poorly defined nodules in cases of measles-associated pneumonia. Additional diagnostic methods include viral isolation using Vero/hSLAM cells and genetic sequencing analysis. There is no specific antiviral therapy for uncomplicated measles. In severe cases, particularly those involving central nervous system (CNS) infection, drugs such as ribavirin and interferon-α have been used. Administration of two doses of vitamin A in children under two years of age has been shown to reduce morbidity and mortality. For most patients, treatment focuses on supportive care. The introduction of the measles vaccine has led to a dramatic reduction in disease incidence. In the United States, widespread vaccination has resulted in a greater than 99% reduction in measles cases compared to the pre-vaccine era. The most effective prevention strategy is active immunization with the measles vaccine, often administered as part of the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine. However, measles remains prevalent in developing countries where vaccination coverage is low. Although there is no specific antiviral treatment for measles, the significant reduction in morbidity and mortality achieved through vaccination underscores its cost-effectiveness. Research efforts continue to focus on developing more effective treatments for established measles cases and improving vaccine accessibility in resource-limited settings. Enhanced vaccination strategies in developing countries could play a critical role in the eventual eradication of measles.
